slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)  ·  Units: g/L, g/dL

What it is used for: A hemoglobin test is most often used to check for anemia, a condition in which the body does not make enough healthy red blood cells. Hemoglobin is usually measured as part of a complete blood count (CBC).

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: The test may be part of a routine exam or ordered for symptoms of anemia (weakness, dizziness, cold hands and feet); a family history of thalassemia, sickle cell anemia or another inherited blood disorder; a diet low in iron and other minerals; a long-term infection; or heavy blood loss from an injury or surgery. It is also used to monitor treatment of anemia and other conditions that affect hemoglobin.

Physiology: Hemoglobin is an iron-rich protein in red blood cells. It carries oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body; cells need oxygen to grow, reproduce and make energy. Hemoglobin levels give information about the health of red blood cells.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result · 1/2
cols: High hemoglobin may be a sign of lung disease, heart disease, polycythemia vera (the bone marrow makes too many red blood cells) or sleep apnea (breathing repeatedly stops during sleep). Living at a higher altitude can also raise hemoglobin.

Low hemoglobin may be a sign of different types of anemia, thalassemia, iron deficiency, liver disease, cancer and other diseases, blood loss from injury, a heavy menstrual period or other problems, or a lack of nutrients such as iron or vitamin B12.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result · 2/2
cols: WHO (2024) also grades anemia severity by hemoglobin. In adults aged 15–65, mild anemia is 110–119 g/L in non-pregnant women and 110–129 g/L in men; moderate is 80–109 g/L; severe is below 80 g/L. In all trimesters of pregnancy, severe anemia is below 70 g/L.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/9
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for a hemoglobin test. If other tests are ordered on the same sample, fasting (no food or drink) for several hours may be required.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/9
bullets: WHO recommends measuring hemoglobin in venous blood on automated hematology analyzers with high-quality control measures. Capillary and venous results clearly differ, but the size of the difference has not been confirmed, so no adjustment is given to make capillary results comparable with venous ones.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/9
bullets: Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, hematology tests use an EDTA tube (usually purple top): EDTA removes calcium by forming calcium salts. The tube needs a full draw and gentle inversion so the blood mixes thoroughly with the additive — poor mixing can give erroneous results. Cap colors may differ by manufacturer.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 4/9
bullets: Interferences: Diet, activity level, certain medicines, dehydration, smoking and certain genetic conditions can affect the result.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 5/9
bullets: WHO recommends adjusting for the elevation of residence above sea level and for smoking when diagnosing anemia: the adjustment is subtracted from the observed hemoglobin or added to the anemia cutoff. For example, the adjustment is 8 g/L for 1000–1499 m and 5 g/L for smoking 10–19 cigarettes a day.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 6/9
bullets: On analysers haemoglobin can be falsely high with lipaemia, marked leukocytosis or paraproteinaemia, which make the lysate turbid. If haemoglobin does not fit the RBC and MCV, the result is checked.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 7/9
bullets: Limitations: The test cannot tell what causes an abnormal level, but how high or low it is helps judge severity. The reference range varies with the laboratory, age, race and sex; results are interpreted with symptoms, history and other blood tests.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 8/9
bullets: The WHO cutoffs are based on the 5th percentile of healthy people: about 5% of healthy individuals have hemoglobin below the cutoff and may be falsely diagnosed as anemic.
A hemoglobin test is not the same as a hemoglobin A1C test, which checks average blood glucose.

slides.title: Hemoglobin (Hb)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 9/9
bullets: The Sahli (acid haematin, visual comparison) method is obsolete: the WHO manual calls the haemiglobincyanide photometric method the most accurate and recommends it wherever possible. Aripova et al. (2007) also note that Sahli is not standardised.

slides.title: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)  ·  Units: fL

What it is used for: MCV is usually part of a complete blood count. Because each type of anemia affects red cell size, shape and quality differently, MCV helps identify the type of anemia together with other tests.
Physiology: MCV measures the average size of red blood cells. Cells that are too small or too large may be a sign of anemia, a lack of certain vitamins or other conditions.
NHLBI reports MCV in femtoliters (fL); a femtoliter is a measure of volume.

slides.title: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result
cols: Larger-than-normal red cells may be a sign of pernicious anemia (from a lack of vitamin B12 or a disease that affects its use, such as certain autoimmune diseases, celiac disease or Crohn’s disease), anemia from a lack of folic acid, or liver disease.

Red cells that are smaller than normal may be a sign of certain anemias, including iron deficiency anemia (the most common form), or of thalassemia (a group of inherited disorders with fewer healthy red cells and less hemoglobin, which can cause severe anemia).

slides.title: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/3
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for this test. If other tests are ordered on the same blood sample, fasting (no food or drink) for several hours may be required.

Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, hematology tests use an EDTA tube (usually purple top): EDTA removes calcium by forming calcium salts. The tube needs a full draw and gentle inversion so the blood mixes thoroughly with the additive — poor mixing can give erroneous results. Cap colors may differ by manufacturer.

slides.title: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/3
bullets: Interferences: Age, diet, activity level, medicines, menstrual period and other conditions can affect MCV; an abnormal value does not always need treatment.

MCV can be falsely high with cold agglutinins, hyperglycaemia and prolonged sample storage (red cells swell; Dolgov et al. cite storage longer than 8 hours). Severe hyponatraemia can falsely lower it. A sudden change that does not fit previous results suggests an error.
Limitations: MCV alone cannot diagnose a disease. Anemia can occur with a normal MCV — for example, after sudden blood loss, in kidney failure or in aplastic anemia.

slides.title: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/3
bullets: Read MCV together with RDW: low MCV with normal RDW — uniform microcytosis (thalassaemia trait, some anaemia of chronic disease); low MCV with high RDW — iron deficiency likely (check ferritin and transferrin saturation); normal MCV with high RDW — mixed populations (early iron deficiency, combined iron + B12/folate deficiency, after transfusion). The reticulocyte count separates poor production from loss or destruction.

slides.title: Mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)

What it is used for: Red blood cell indices are part of a complete blood count and are used to diagnose different types of anemia, each of which affects red cell size, shape and/or quality differently. The test is done at routine checkups or for symptoms of anemia (shortness of breath, weakness, headache, dizziness, arrhythmia, pale skin, cold hands and feet).

Physiology: MCH measures the average amount of hemoglobin in a single red blood cell. It is one of the red cell indices, which assess red cell size, shape and quality and help identify the type of anemia.

slides.title: Mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result
cols: A higher-than-normal MCH may point to anemia caused by a vitamin B deficiency.
A lower-than-normal MCH may point to iron deficiency anemia.

slides.title: Mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for this test.

Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, hematology tests use an EDTA tube (usually purple top): EDTA removes calcium by forming calcium salts. The tube needs a full draw and gentle inversion so the blood mixes thoroughly with the additive — poor mixing can give erroneous results. Cap colors may differ by manufacturer.
Limitations: Index results are interpreted with symptoms, medical history and other blood tests; abnormal indices may point to some type of anemia, but the diagnosis is made by the provider.

slides.title: Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)
Physiology: MCHC measures how concentrated (close together) hemoglobin is in red blood cells; it also includes a calculation of red cell size and volume.

slides.title: Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result
cols: A high MCHC may be a sign of hemolytic anemia (red cells are destroyed faster than they can be replaced) or hereditary spherocytosis (a rare genetic disorder causing anemia and gallstones).
A low MCHC may point to iron deficiency anemia or thalassemia.

slides.title: Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/3
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for this test.

Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, hematology tests use an EDTA tube (usually purple top): EDTA removes calcium by forming calcium salts. The tube needs a full draw and gentle inversion so the blood mixes thoroughly with the additive — poor mixing can give erroneous results. Cap colors may differ by manufacturer.

slides.title: Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/3
bullets: Interferences: MCHC changes very little physiologically, so it is a sensitive marker of measurement error. Takami (2026) treats MCHC above 36 g/dL (360 g/L) as suggesting artefact; Dolgov et al. give 37–38 g/dL. Causes: falsely high Hb (lipaemia, leukocytosis) or falsely low RBC (cold agglutinins). A truly high MCHC occurs in spherocytosis. False lowering: hyperglycaemia and prolonged storage.

slides.title: Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/3
bullets: Limitations: Index results are interpreted with symptoms, medical history and other blood tests; abnormal indices may point to some type of anemia, but the diagnosis is made by the provider.
The “colour index” of former-USSR textbooks is an old, hand-calculated counterpart of MCH (mean cell haemoglobin); Dolgov et al. consider it obsolete. Analysers report MCH, MCHC and MCV directly.

slides.title: Red cell distribution width (RDW)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)  ·  Units: %

What it is used for: RDW is often part of a complete blood count and is commonly used to help diagnose anemia or find its cause; with other tests it also helps diagnose conditions such as thalassemia.
Physiology: RDW measures how much the volume and size of red blood cells vary. Normally red cells are about the same size; differences may affect how well they deliver oxygen.
RDW uses a special graph called a histogram: when red cells are about the same size they sit close together on it and the RDW is low; when sizes are spread out, the RDW is high.

slides.title: Red cell distribution width (RDW)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result
cols: A high RDW means red cell sizes vary more than normal. It may be a sign of chronic liver disease, heart disease, diabetes, kidney disease or cancer, especially colorectal cancer.
A low RDW means red cells are similar in size; it is not a sign of anemia and usually not a concern.

slides.title: Red cell distribution width (RDW)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/2
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for this test.

Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, hematology tests use an EDTA tube (usually purple top): EDTA removes calcium by forming calcium salts. The tube needs a full draw and gentle inversion so the blood mixes thoroughly with the additive — poor mixing can give erroneous results. Cap colors may differ by manufacturer.

slides.title: Red cell distribution width (RDW)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/2
bullets: Limitations: Results are usually shown as a percentage and compared with a reference range that varies by lab. Even with a normal RDW, red cells may be larger or smaller than usual and anemia may be present. RDW is read together with other blood tests, which together help diagnose iron deficiency, different anemias, thalassemia and sickle cell anemia.
RDW alone is not enough for a diagnosis, so it is combined with other indices and blood tests.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 1/3
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (hematology EDTA tube); heel-stick capillary blood in newborns  ·  Units: %

What it is used for: The count is most often used to diagnose specific types of anemia, see whether anemia treatment is working, check whether the bone marrow makes enough red cells, and check marrow function after chemotherapy or a bone marrow transplant.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 2/3
bullets: It is ordered when other tests (CBC, hemoglobin, hematocrit) show abnormal red cell levels, during radiation or chemotherapy, after a recent bone marrow transplant and for symptoms of anemia. Newborns may be tested for hemolytic disease of the newborn, which can occur with Rh incompatibility between mother and baby.

Physiology: Reticulocytes are immature (still developing) red blood cells made in the bone marrow; they enter the blood and mature into red cells within one to two days. The count checks whether the marrow makes the right amount of red cells as old ones die off.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 3/3
bullets: Modern analysers do more than count reticulocytes: they measure maturity by RNA content (the fraction of the youngest cells — IRF), cell volume and haemoglobin content (RET-He or CHr). Names, method and reference ranges depend on the analyser.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result · 1/2
cols: Reticulocytosis (a high count) may mean hemolytic anemia (red cells are destroyed faster than the marrow can replace them), new or ongoing bleeding (the body makes many more red cells to replace those lost), or hemolytic disease of the newborn.

A low count may mean iron deficiency anemia, pernicious anemia (a megaloblastic anemia from too little or poorly absorbed vitamin B12 and folate), aplastic anemia (the marrow cannot make enough blood cells), bone marrow failure from infection or cancer, kidney disease or cirrhosis.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result · 2/2
cols: IRF is an early marker of marrow activity: after stem-cell transplantation it shows erythroid recovery before the total reticulocyte count does; Dolgov et al. also cite it as an early sign of response to anaemia treatment.

Reticulocyte haemoglobin content (RET-He, CHr) indirectly reflects the functional iron available for red cell production over the previous 3–4 days; a low value points to iron-restricted erythropoiesis. The cut-off depends on the analyser and laboratory — use the reference on the report.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/7
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed. Adults give a vein sample; in newborns the heel is pricked with a small needle.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/7
bullets: Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, hematology tests use an EDTA tube (usually purple top): EDTA removes calcium by forming calcium salts. The tube needs a full draw and gentle inversion so the blood mixes thoroughly with the additive — poor mixing can give erroneous results. Cap colors may differ by manufacturer.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/7
bullets: Interferences: Reticulocyte counts may be higher during pregnancy; they rise for a short time after moving to a high altitude and return to normal once the body adjusts. Some medicines may increase or decrease the count.

On analysers reticulocytes can be falsely high because of nucleated red cells (NRBCs), red-cell inclusions or fluorescent interference; with an analyser flag or a result that does not fit the clinical picture, check the smear.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 4/7
bullets: Limitations: To understand the result, the provider considers symptoms, history and other blood tests; an abnormal count does not always mean anemia or another condition.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 5/7
bullets: In anaemia the absolute count or a haematocrit-corrected index (CRC, RPI) is used instead of the percentage. Takami (2026) gives approximate adult guides: above about 80×10⁹/L suggests an increased marrow response (bleeding, haemolysis, recovery); below about 20×10⁹/L with severe anaemia suggests markedly impaired erythropoiesis. These are not rigid diagnostic cut-offs.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 6/7
bullets: MSCV (mean sphered cell volume) is reported only by some analysers (per the source, Beckman Coulter). In hereditary spherocytosis MSCV is usually lower than MCV, which helps separate it from thalassaemia; the diagnosis is confirmed with the smear, family studies and other tests.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 7/7
bullets: Manual counting uses a supravital stain (e.g., brilliant cresyl blue) and relates reticulocytes to red cells (traditionally per 1000). Since the 1990s automated flow-cytometric counting has replaced microscopy: it is more accurate and precise, but results are not fully standardised between laboratories.

slides.title: Hematocrit (HCT)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)  ·  Units: %

What it is used for: Hematocrit is often part of a complete blood count. It is used to check general health and to help diagnose or monitor blood disorders such as anemia (too few red blood cells) and polycythemia (erythrocytosis, an uncommon disorder with too many red blood cells and blood that becomes too thick).

slides.title: Hematocrit (HCT)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: The test may be part of a routine checkup, monitoring during cancer treatment or an ongoing condition, or ordered for symptoms of anemia (shortness of breath, weakness, headache, dizziness, arrhythmia) or of polycythemia (headache, shortness of breath when lying down, itching after a shower, a red face, heavy sweating especially during sleep, blurred vision, unusual bleeding from the gums or nose).

Physiology: Hematocrit measures what percent of the blood is made up of red blood cells. The rest is white blood cells, platelets and a liquid called plasma. For example, a result of 42 means 42% of the blood is red blood cells.

slides.title: Hematocrit (HCT)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result
cols: A high hematocrit may come from making too many red blood cells (lung disease, congenital heart disease, heart failure, polycythemia) or from low blood plasma due to dehydration (the most common cause of a high hematocrit) or shock. Living at a high altitude also raises it, because the body makes more red cells when oxygen is low.

A low hematocrit may be a sign of recent blood loss from an injury, chronic blood loss, anemia or the body making too many white blood cells (bone marrow disease, leukemia, lymphoma, multiple myeloma or cancer that has spread to the bone marrow). Pregnancy can lower the hematocrit because the body holds more fluid.

slides.title: Hematocrit (HCT)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/2
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for this test. If other tests are ordered on the same blood sample, fasting (no food or drink) for several hours may be required.

Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, hematology tests use an EDTA tube (usually purple top): EDTA removes calcium by forming calcium salts. The tube needs a full draw and gentle inversion so the blood mixes thoroughly with the additive — poor mixing can give erroneous results. Cap colors may differ by manufacturer.

slides.title: Hematocrit (HCT)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/2
bullets: Interferences: On analysers haematocrit is often not measured directly — it approximates the product of the red cell count and MCV. So an error in RBC or MCV (e.g., cold agglutinins, hyperglycaemia, prolonged storage) carries over to the haematocrit.

Limitations: Normal hematocrit varies with sex, age, smoking and the altitude where one lives — compare with the interval on the lab report and discuss with the provider. A result outside the range does not always mean a condition that needs treatment.

slides.title: Anaemia: step-by-step work-up
slides.eyebrow: Condition · Overview
bullets: Anaemia is a sign, not a diagnosis: it is detected by haemoglobin, then MCV (red cell size) classifies it as microcytic, normocytic or macrocytic, and reticulocytes show the marrow response. Further tests follow from these two steps: iron studies, B12/folate or markers of haemolysis.

slides.title: Anaemia: step-by-step work-up
slides.eyebrow: Condition · Tests to consider · 1/3
rows: Detects anaemia and grades severity; WHO cut-offs depend on age, sex and pregnancy.
MCV classifies anaemia by cell size; RDW reveals mixed populations.
Marrow response: high — bleeding or haemolysis; low — impaired production.

slides.title: Anaemia: step-by-step work-up
slides.eyebrow: Condition · Tests to consider · 2/3
rows: First test in microcytic anaemia: a low ferritin confirms iron deficiency.
Help separate iron deficiency from anaemia of inflammation.
In macrocytic anaemia, to look for megaloblastic causes.

slides.title: Anaemia: step-by-step work-up
slides.eyebrow: Condition · Tests to consider · 3/3
rows: Haemolysis markers: LDH, indirect bilirubin, haptoglobin
With high reticulocytes and no bleeding — to confirm haemolysis.
Red cell shape (spherocytes, schistocytes, target cells) points to the cause.

slides.title: Anaemia: step-by-step work-up
slides.eyebrow: Condition · Result patterns · 1/3
rows: Microcytic anaemia: most often iron deficiency, also thalassaemia. Check ferritin and iron studies.
Iron-deficiency anaemia likely; the cause (blood loss etc.) is sought. WHO (2020): ferritin <15 µg/L in healthy adults or <70 µg/L with inflammation indicates iron deficiency.
Microcytosis, normal ferritin, normal RDW, relatively preserved RBC count
Thalassaemia trait possible — haemoglobin variant testing.

slides.title: Anaemia: step-by-step work-up
slides.eyebrow: Condition · Result patterns · 2/3
rows: Active marrow: recent bleeding or haemolysis. Check haemolysis markers (LDH, bilirubin, haptoglobin) and the smear.
Normal MCV, low or normal reticulocytes

Reduced production: anaemia of chronic disease (inflammation), kidney disease, marrow disease or early mixed deficiency. With severe anaemia and very low reticulocytes, marrow failure must be excluded (investigated).

slides.title: Anaemia: step-by-step work-up
slides.eyebrow: Condition · Result patterns · 3/3
rows: Macrocytic anaemia: B12 or folate deficiency (RDW often high), also alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, some medicines, myelodysplasia. Check B12 and folate.

slides.title: Anaemia: step-by-step work-up
slides.eyebrow: Condition · Cautions
bullets: The algorithm is a guide: with mixed deficiencies MCV can be normal, and numeric cut-offs are approximate and laboratory-dependent. First make sure the result is genuine (spurious results: Learn → Tables and algorithms). The final judgement is the doctor’s.

slides.title: 1. Is there anaemia?
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Anaemia: step by step
bullets: Defined by haemoglobin. WHO (2024): <120 g/L in non-pregnant women aged 15–65, <130 g/L in men; cut-offs are adjusted for age, pregnancy, altitude and smoking.
First check that the result is genuine — see “Analyser spurious results”.

slides.title: 2. Type by MCV
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Anaemia: step by step
bullets: Low MCV (≈ <80 fL): Microcytic: mostly iron deficiency; thalassaemia → ferritin, iron studies
Normal MCV: Normocytic: acute blood loss, kidney disease, chronic disease, aplastic anaemia → reticulocytes decide
High MCV (≈ >100 fL): Macrocytic: B12 or folate deficiency, liver disease, alcohol, hypothyroidism → B12, folate

slides.title: 3. Marrow response — reticulocytes
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Anaemia: step by step
bullets: High (≈ >80×10⁹/L): Bleeding, haemolysis or recovery after treatment → haemolysis markers
Low (≈ <20×10⁹/L with severe anaemia): Poor production: deficiencies, kidney, marrow disease
Cut-offs are approximate; use the absolute count or a corrected index (CRC, RPI) rather than the percentage.

slides.title: MCV with RDW
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Anaemia: step by step
bullets: MCV ↓, RDW normal: Thalassaemia trait, some anaemia of chronic disease
MCV ↓, RDW ↑: Iron deficiency (ferritin, transferrin saturation)
MCV normal, RDW ↑: Early iron deficiency, mixed deficiency, after transfusion
MCV ↑, RDW ↑: B12 or folate deficiency, myelodysplasia

slides.title: Iron: deficiency or inflammation?
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Anaemia: step by step
bullets: Iron deficiency: Ferritin ↓, iron ↓, transferrin saturation ↓, TIBC usually ↑
Anaemia of inflammation: Iron ↓, TIBC ↓, ferritin normal or ↑
Ferritin cut-off (WHO 2020): Healthy adults <15 µg/L; with inflammation <70 µg/L (with CRP, AGP)

slides.title: Haemolysis markers
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Anaemia: step by step
bullets: Reticulocytes ↑, LDH ↑, indirect bilirubin ↑, haptoglobin ↓.
The Coombs (antiglobulin) test identifies immune haemolysis; spherocytes suggest a membrane defect, schistocytes thrombotic microangiopathy.
A marked LDH rise with haemosiderinuria — intravascular haemolysis.

slides.title: Example: MCHC
slides.eyebrow: Example
bullets: Formula: MCHC (g/dL) = Hb (g/dL) ÷ Hct (%) × 100

slides.title: According to WHO (2024), below which hemoglobin level is a non-pregnant woman aged 15–65 considered anemic?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the cutoff for non-pregnant women aged 15–65 is 120 g/L (12.0 g/dL).

Basis: WHO Table 2: non-pregnant women < 120 g/L (12.0 g/dL), men < 130 g/L (13.0 g/dL), first and third trimesters < 110 g/L (11.0 g/dL).

slides.title: A patient lives 1,200 m above sea level. What does WHO recommend when assessing anemia?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
options: An adjustment — 8 g/L (0.8 g/dL) — is added to the cutoff
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: or it is subtracted from the observed value — same result.

Basis: The altitude adjustment — 8 g/L (0.8 g/dL) for 1000–1499 m — is subtracted from observed hemoglobin or added to the anemia cutoff.

slides.title: A hematocrit result is 0.42 L/L (42%). What does it mean?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
options: 42% of the blood is red cells
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the rest is white cells, platelets and plasma.

Basis: Hematocrit is the percentage of blood made up of red blood cells.

slides.title: According to the source, what is the most common cause of a high hematocrit?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the source calls it the most common cause.

Basis: Low plasma — mainly dehydration — raises the hematocrit.

slides.title: MCV is low (small red cells). Which causes does the source give?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct.

Basis: Small cells: iron deficiency anemia, thalassemia. Large: B12/folate deficiency, liver disease.

slides.title: MCV is normal. Does that rule out anemia?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
options: Yes, a normal MCV rules it out
No, e.g. after sudden blood loss
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct.

Basis: Anemia can occur with a normal MCV: sudden blood loss, kidney failure, aplastic anemia.

slides.title: Anemias. Classification, etiology and pathogenesis?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 1/3
bullets: 1. Anemia is a decrease in Hb below the norm for age, sex and physiological state (per WHO approximately <130 g/L in men, <120 g/L in non-pregnant women); insufficient oxygen transport.

2. Pathogenetic classification: 1) blood loss (acute, chronic); 2) impaired erythropoiesis – iron, B12/folate deficiency, anemia of chronic disease (inflammation), bone marrow failure (aplasia, MDS, infiltration), kidney disease; 3) increased destruction of erythrocytes – hemolytic (inherited: membranopathies, enzymopathies, hemoglobinopathies; acquired: immune, mechanical, infectious, toxic).

slides.title: Anemias. Classification, etiology and pathogenesis?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 2/3
bullets: 3. Morphological classification by MCV: microcytic (<80 fL), normocytic (80–100), macrocytic (>100); by MCH/MCHC – hypo-/normochromic; RDW as an addition.
4. By bone marrow response: reticulocytes increased (regenerative – hemolysis, blood loss) or low (hyporegenerative – impaired production); assessed with RPI.

slides.title: Anemias. Classification, etiology and pathogenesis?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 3/3
bullets: 5. Laboratory algorithm: CBC + indices + reticulocytes + smear → in microcytosis ferritin/TSAT; in macrocytosis B12, folate (MMA if needed); in normocytosis signs of hemolysis (LDH, indirect bilirubin, haptoglobin, direct antiglobulin test), kidney function, inflammation.

slides.title: Anemias accompanied by iron deficiency?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 1/2
bullets: 1. Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) is the most common anemia; causes: chronic blood loss (menorrhagia in women, GI bleeding), increased demand (pregnancy, growth), malabsorption (celiac disease, gastrectomy, H. pylori), inadequate dietary intake.
2. Stages: first the stores are depleted (ferritin↓), then iron delivery is impaired (TSAT↓, CHr↓), and finally Hb falls – Hb is a late sign.

3. Laboratory criteria: ferritin <30 ng/mL or TSAT <20% – absolute iron deficiency (StatPearls); AGA/ASH recommend ferritin <45 ng/mL for IDA; WHO 2020: <15 µg/L in healthy adults, <70 µg/L in infection/inflammation; serum iron varies through the day and is unreliable alone.

slides.title: Anemias accompanied by iron deficiency?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 2/2
bullets: 4. Blood: microcytic hypochromic anemia, RDW↑, anisopoikilocytosis, "pencil" cells, target cells; reticulocytes low/normal; thrombocytosis may occur.
5. Differentiation: thalassemia trait (ferritin normal, RDW often normal, Hb electrophoresis), anemia of chronic disease (ferritin normal/high), sideroblastic anemia.
6. Response to treatment: 1–2 weeks after iron is given, reticulocytes rise, then Hb; looking for the cause (source of bleeding) is mandatory.

slides.title: Bone marrow and peripheral blood picture in anemias accompanied by iron deficiency?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 1/2
bullets: 1. Peripheral blood: Hb decreased, MCV <80 fL, MCH and MCHC low (hypochromia), RDW increased; the smear shows microcytes, anisopoikilocytosis, elliptocytes ("pencil" cells), target cells.
2. Reticulocytes normal or low (absolute count low), CHr/Ret-He <28 pg; platelets often normal or reactively increased.

3. Bone marrow (rarely needed for diagnosis): erythroid hyperplasia, predominance of small early erythroid cells with "ragged" cytoplasm; with Perls stain (Prussian blue) there is no iron in macrophages and sideroblasts are sharply reduced.

slides.title: Bone marrow and peripheral blood picture in anemias accompanied by iron deficiency?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline · 2/2
bullets: 4. Bone marrow iron is the gold standard for assessing stores, but invasive; in practice replaced by ferritin and TSAT.
5. Differentiation: in anemia of chronic disease, iron in bone marrow macrophages is preserved/increased; in sideroblastic anemia – ring sideroblasts.
